results.title: Intriguing place
results.text: Pashupatinath is a hindu temple area built on the banks of the river where cremations take place. It is said to have been built on a sacred site where Shiva and Parvati mated in the form of animals. It is a highly worshipped place and many big and small temples have been built over the centuries. results.title: Take some time for this Holy abode
results.text:
It was the first visit to Nepal and since it was a business trip didn't had much time in hand for sightseeing. But Pashupatinath temple was un-missable. It's very close to Kathmandu airport.
Now, if you are visiting here, make sure you have at-least an hour's time just for main temple courtyard. It's almost nothing like ever seen. From main entrance, you can only see a huge bronze Nandi's back. Since camera not allowed, this is the only view you can click of the inner part. There are many small cupolas around with idols in the courtyard. There are lot many steps where you can peacefully sit and even meditate.
The main temple itself is amazing. Probably completely made of wood and stone, with beautiful stone and wood carved figurines of Devatas. The two story building with these features is mesmerizing. The view of the main Shivalinga is through a very small door. Take enough time to look at it if there's not much crowd. The inside is only lit by Diyas.
Behind and around the main temple are other structures with idols. Just behind the temple and downwards flows Bhagmati river and there is also an area for cremation of bodies. On the opposite side of the river, again there is a line of beautiful small cupolas in front of which Aarti of Bhagmati river is held. Somewhat similar to Ganga Aarti in Kashi. From here only you can click the proper pics of main temple building.
Overall it's a very soulful and peaceful experience especially being among the old and beautiful structures.
You may take a guide too but I was not having much time so left the option. Lots of monkeys around! Careful while carrying the Prasad packets.

results.title: authentic and humbling
results.text: Ended up spending about 2-3 solid hours here.  Make sure to walk around to the riverfront.  We almost didn't!  It isn't clear that you can walk that way because the ground is all muddy and not paved, and sort of a mess (maybe due to last year's earthquake, but I'm really not sure).  It cost us 1000 rupees each for entrance.  You can't enter the actual temple unless you are Hindu, but the cremations are going on 24/7 and being able to watch this process from across the river was pretty incredible.  The ritual has so many steps.  It was all performed in a way that made me feel like i was watching a celebration of life, rather than watching mourning of a death. It was beautiful and completely different than anything I had ever experienced before.  Be careful of the hippie priests hanging around, they lure you in for photos and then ask for steep donations in return!  Otherwise, visiting this temple was a highlight of our trip to Nepal.

results.title: An amazing place for contemplation and reflection .....
results.text:
Pashupatinath temple is the most important temple dedicated to lord Shiva in Nepal and one of its most scared Hindu temples. Located on the banks of the holly Bagmati river (which much further down flows into the Ganges) and at about five km from Kathmandu, Pashupathinath is the place where Hindus from both Nepal and India come to die and be cremated, in the belief that dying in Pashupathinath guarantees their rebirth not as a worm, a pig or a dog, but as human, irrespective of the misdeeds in their lives... You can, of course, observe the bodies being brought to the cremation ghats, the oldest son pouring some incents and holly water from the river before lighting the funeral pyre, then ashes being discarded into the holly Baghmati and further down the river kids playing into the water and women doing their laundry. Here, death is not the end but just another step towards Nirvana.... 
The temple itself (available only to Hindus) is a masterpiece of Hindu architecture and, if you are interested in religions, in other ways of thinking of life and death, then you may not like to miss a visit Pashupatinath.. .

results.title: Authentic cultural experience
results.text:
The best time to go is 5:30 pm. Go for the interest of the cultural differences, explore the temple grounds, and stay for the Aarti ceremony, which starts at 7pm. You will want to be seated by 6 pm for the ceremony. I think it lasts an hour. It was definitely an authentic experience I truly enjoyed the Aarti. 

Seeing the burning ghats and basically "attending" a Hindi funeral was quite powerful and felt almost intrusive; however, coming to the temple and watching the "funerals" is what many people (including locals) do. Oddly enough. 

I never hired a guide, but wish I would have. Apparently one of the Mother Theresa homes is nearby and part of the guided "tour." 

I have found temple guides to be very hot or miss. When they don't know information, sometimes they make it up. It is best to check with your hotel and see if they recommend anyone. 

Also, taxis in Nepal are crooks. Be prepared to haggle and stick to your guns. I am hoping Ola cabs or Uber will come to give them competition.

results.title: Worth visiting, though strict rules on entry
results.text:
Pashupati Temple is beautiful, with lovely grounds especially at sunset, but only Hindus are allowed in the temple itself, so many westerners and tourists will not be allowed in the temple proper. 

There are some scammers around as well - "shamans" who dress in full traditional attire and demand money, then try to "curse" you if you don't give them a donation. These men are not genuine, and you should not feel pressured to donate to them, even when they hold swords to your throat. Just be firm and walk away.
